title: The interactive J-lens viewer
takeaway: The figure is the live tool the authors used throughout the work: a grid of top-ranked lens tokens over every (position, layer) cell of a forward pass, with pinned-token heatmaps and rank trajectories. On a prompt asking Sonnet 4.5 to count to five while introspecting, it surfaces counting progress markers and introspection concepts that never appear in the model's text.
walkthrough:
This item is not a static picture. It is a working copy of the [[j-lens-visualization]], the interactive tool the authors used throughout their research, embedded in the article for the reader to operate.

The display is organized around a grid with two axes. One axis runs over token positions: the tokens of the prompt and of the model's response, in order. The other runs over layers: depth in the model's [[residual-stream]]. Each cell of the grid therefore names one activation — one position, one layer.

The left column holds the prompt at the top, then a hoverable table showing, for each cell, the single top-ranked token of the [[j-lens-readout]] at that activation. The readout is the basic operation of the [[jacobian-lens]]: it scores every vocabulary token by how disposed that activation is, averaged across contexts, to make the model say it. Below the table sits a heatmap. A reader can pin a token of interest, and the heatmap records that token's rank in every cell, so one concept can be traced across the whole pass at once.

The other columns give depth. The middle column shows the full ranked readout across all layers at one selected position; the right column shows it across all positions at one selected layer. Line charts trace each pinned token's rank trajectory. The reading practice is: skim the top-1 grid for unexpected tokens, pin them, and use the heatmaps and trajectories to see where in depth and position they are active.

The example prompt asks Sonnet 4.5, one of the [[claude-model-family]], to "Count to five and introspect deeply." The output text just counts. The lens shows more. Pinned tokens show the model identifying the task as counting and tracking progress with halfway and done — tokens that appear in neither the prompt nor the output. Alongside them, introspection concepts — thoughts, AI, claude, consciousness — cluster near the top, held in the [[j-space]] in response to the instruction while the surface task runs. In the final few layers the readout flips to the predicted next token: the [[motor-layers]] regime. In roughly the first third of the model, the [[sensory-layers]], readouts are noisy and largely uninterpretable.

Further interactive examples ship with the article, and readouts on open-source models are hosted on Neuronpedia as part of the [[j-lens-open-source-release]].

terms.definition: One axis of the grid: the index of a token in the prompt-plus-response sequence. Each position has its own residual-stream activation at every layer.
The other axis of the grid: depth in the model's residual stream. The paper reports layers as percentages of depth, sampled at evenly spaced points.
One entry of the grid, corresponding to one activation vector; the viewer shows the top-ranked J-lens token for each such cell.
The scoring of every vocabulary token against one activation, softmax(W_U norm(J_l h_l)); the top of the ranking names what the activation disposes the model to say.
The single highest-scoring vocabulary token of a cell's readout; the hoverable table shows only this token per cell.
A token the user selects for tracking; the viewer then records its rank in every cell rather than only where it is top-ranked.
The bottom-left panel: a color map over all (position, layer) cells showing each pinned token's rank, so a concept's footprint across the pass is visible at once.
A line chart tracing a pinned token's rank as one axis varies, showing where in depth or position the concept rises toward the top of the readout.
The middle column: the full ranked readout across all layers at one chosen token position.
The right column: the readout across all token positions at one chosen layer.
The production Claude model the example runs on; Sonnet is the middle size tier of the family the paper studies.
The example prompt: a trivial surface task paired with an instruction to introspect, so the lens can be compared against output text that only counts.
Progress-marker tokens surfaced by the lens while the model counts; they appear in neither the prompt nor the output, illustrating contextual awareness the lens can expose.
Introspection-related tokens clustering near the top of the readout — concepts held in the workspace in response to the instruction, without being said.
The final few layers, where the readout flips from workspace content to the predicted next token that is about to be emitted.
A token's place in the sorted readout at one cell; rank 1 means the readout scores it above every other vocabulary token there.
The article's own gallery of further interactive J-lens examples beyond this one.
The hosted platform where an interactive version of the lens, applied to open-source models, is publicly available.

numbers.meaning: The count target in the example prompt. The surface task is made trivial on purpose, so the interesting content of the readout is what the model holds beyond its output.
Each cell of the hoverable table shows only the single highest-ranked readout token; the full ranking is available in the per-position and per-layer columns.
Roughly the first third of the model's layers give noisy, largely uninterpretable readouts — the sensory band, where the paper says the J-space is essentially empty.
Where the readout flips to the predicted next token — the motor regime — so workspace content is read off in the middle layers, not at the end.
The version number of the Sonnet model the example runs on.
